subject: immune-system
title: Your Body's Germ Defense Team
summary: How your skin, white blood cells and antibodies team up to fight germs.

keys.answer: They remember a germ your body fought before. If it comes back, your body can fight it faster.

options.text: Help your body fight a germ faster the next time
Chew up germs that get into a cut
Make your skin into a stronger wall

keys.prompt: How does a vaccine help your body?
keys.answer: It shows your body a germ in a safe way, so your body learns to spot it without you getting sick.

options.text: It lets your body learn about a germ safely
It gives you the sickness to get it over with
It kills all the germs in your body

keys.answer: They are white blood cells that chew up germs that get past your skin.

options.text: They chew up germs
They make antibodies
They make mucus to trap germs

cards.title: Germs on the doorknob
cards.text: Think about what you touched today, like a doorknob. Each time, you came close to germs. So why aren't you sick all the time? Your body has a defense team, and it is always on duty.

cards.question: Say the same germ gets into your body a second time. What do you think happens?

options.text: Your body fights it faster than the first time
Your body has to start over from scratch
Your body doesn't notice it at all

cards.reveal: It fights faster! Some of your germ fighters remember the germ. Next time your body can fight back fast, and often you don't get sick at all.

cards.title: Walls come first
cards.text: Your first defense is a wall: your skin. Sticky mucus traps germs. Your tears and skin oils have germ-fighting helpers. Stomach acid helps too, and a cough can push germs out.
cards.example: Your skin works like the wall around a castle. Germs have to get past it first.

why.q: Why is a wall a smart first defense?
why.a: It keeps lots of germs out before they get in. Then your body has fewer germs to fight.

cards.title: The germ eaters
cards.text: If germs get past the walls, white blood cells fight back. Some, called phagocytes (FAH-guh-sites), chew up germs. You can find white blood cells in your bone marrow. That is the thick, spongy jelly inside your bones.
cards.example: Did a small cut ever get a bit puffy? Hurt cells send out signals. The signals make the spot swell, and they call the germ eaters in.

cards.title: Antibodies lock on
cards.text: Other white blood cells, called B cells, make antibodies. An antibody locks onto one kind of germ, like a key that fits one lock. Antibodies can't destroy germs by themselves. They mark germs, so other cells can destroy them.

cards.title: Germ fighters remember
cards.text: After a fight, a few B cells and T cells stay on as memory cells. If the same germ comes back, they know it. Your body can fight back faster. Often, you don't get sick at all.
cards.example: That's why someone who had chickenpox usually won't get it again.

why.q: Why can your body fight a germ faster the second time?
why.a: Memory cells already know that germ. So your body doesn't have to start over.

cards.title: Vaccines are practice
cards.text: A vaccine shows your body a germ in a safe way. It might have germs that are dead or weak, or just a piece of a germ. Your body learns to spot it and makes memory cells. Then you are ready if the real germ shows up.
cards.example: The measles shot, for example, can protect you from getting measles.

cards.question: Your defense team has walls, germ eaters, antibody makers and memory cells. If you could keep only one, which would you pick? Why?
nudges: What would happen without the walls?
What if your body forgot every germ it ever fought?

questions.q: What is your body's first defense against germs?

options.text: Walls like your skin and sticky mucus
options.why: Right! They keep lots of germs out before they get in.

options.text: Memory cells
options.why: Memory cells help later, once your body has met a germ before.

options.text: Vaccines
options.why: Vaccines help your body practice. But your skin is the first wall.

options.text: They lock onto a germ so other cells can destroy it
options.why: Yes! They mark the germ for the rest of the team.

options.text: They chew up germs
They make your skin thicker
options.why: Antibodies lock onto germs. They don't change your skin.

questions.q: How does a vaccine help you?

options.text: It teaches your body about a germ without making you sick
options.why: Right. Your body makes memory cells, so it is ready.

options.text: It cleans every germ out of your body
options.why: A vaccine trains your body for a certain germ. It is practice, not a cleaner.

options.text: It makes you sick so you rest
options.why: A vaccine is given in a way that doesn't make you sick.

sources.title: Immune response
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, NIH)
sources.supports: Innate immunity's barriers are the first line of defense: the cough reflex, enzymes in tears and skin oils, mucus that traps bacteria, skin, and stomach acid; damaged cells release chemicals that make blood vessels leak fluid (swelling) and attract phagocytes that "eat" germs; B cells make antibodies that attach to a specific antigen and make it easier for immune cells to destroy it; a few B and T cells provide "memory" so the body responds faster next time and in many cases you don't get sick; vaccines give small doses of an antigen, such as dead or weakened viruses or parts of a virus, to activate that memory.

sources.title: Your Immune System (for Kids)
sources.supports: White blood cells (leukocytes) include phagocytes, which chew up invading germs, and lymphocytes, which help the body remember and recognize invaders; leukocytes are found in bone marrow, a thick, spongy jelly inside your bones; the measles shot can protect you from getting measles.

sources.title: The Immune System (for Teens)
sources.supports: Touching things like a bathroom doorknob exposes you to germs; skin is a barrier that blocks germs; phagocytes such as neutrophils chew up invaders; B cells make antibodies that lock onto specific antigens; antibodies can't destroy a germ without help; T cells destroy infected cells and signal other cells like phagocytes; B cells compared to military intelligence and T cells to soldiers; someone who had chickenpox usually won't get it again; vaccines introduce an antigen in a way that doesn't make someone sick; innate, adaptive (active) and passive immunity, with antibodies in breast milk as borrowed, short-lived protection.
